source_text: Denique statim addit, ita eos servos esse iustitiae, sicut fuerant servi ante peccati. Per quod potes eos iam tu, si placet, liberos dicere peccato, cum serviunt iustitiae; sicut ab illo dicti sunt a iustitia liberi, cum servirent delicto. Ineptissime itaque simplicitati apostolicae voluisti calumniam commovere. Neque enim ille, ut putas, vigilantissime hoc quod aestimas intimavit; sed tu somniculosissime quod ille protulit intueris. Argumentaris quippe, ideo illum liberatos dicere maluisse, quam liberos, ut intellegeremus arbitrii libertate male quidem posse, bene autem fieri non posse. Verum ipse tibi verborum eius ordo renititur. Nam si hoc, quod tu, putasset, quia libertate solum peccaretur, debuit dicere: Liberi fuistis peccato; non: Liberi fuistis iustitiae [n288] , ut ille diceretur esse liber, cui operabatur ipsa libertas. Si enim placet etiam casuum pensare momenta, huic illos iustitiae dixit esse liberos, non ab hac iustitia liberos. Consequentius ergo hac elocutione nos adiuvaremur, si etiam tam leves res premere vellemus. Sed absit hoc: sensum intellegimus Apostoli, et elocutionum simpliciter prolatarum officio contenti sumus. Nihil aliud dixit Magister Gentium, nisi: Liberi fuistis, non servistis, iustitiae; liberati estis, peccatorum veniam suscepistis, manente arbitrii libertate; per quam potuerunt et ante peccato, et postea oboedire iustitiae.
pass_a_gloss: Finally at once he adds, that they are so slaves of justice, as they had been slaves of sin before. Through which you can already, if it pleases, say them free to sin, when they serve justice; as by him they have been said free from justice, when they were serving the fault. Most ineptly therefore you wanted to move a calumny to apostolic simplicity. For neither did he, as you think, most vigilantly intimate this which you estimate; but you most sleepily look at what he brought forth. You argue indeed, that therefore he preferred to say freed, rather than free, that we might understand that by liberty of choice it is possible indeed badly, but cannot be made well. But the very order of his words resists you. For if he had thought this, which you, because by liberty alone it was sinned, he ought to have said: You were free to sin; not: You were free of justice, that he would be said to be free, for whom that liberty itself was working. For if it pleases also to weigh the moments of cases, he said those to be free to this justice, not free from this justice. More consequently therefore by this expression we would be helped, if we also wanted to press such light things. But far be this: we understand the sense of the Apostle, and we are content with the office of expressions brought forth simply. The Teacher of the Nations said nothing other, except: You were free, you did not serve, justice; you have been freed, you have taken up pardon of sins, with the liberty of choice remaining; through which they could both before obey sin, and afterward justice.

lemmas.lexica: LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS arbitrium=judgment, free decision; Blaise liberum arbitrium
LS libertas; Blaise moral freedom to will or refuse

pass_b_english: He immediately adds that they are slaves of righteousness in the same way that they had previously been slaves of sin. You may now, if you wish, call them free from sin when they serve righteousness, just as he called them free from righteousness when they served wrongdoing. Most foolishly, then, you wanted to bring an accusation against the apostle's straightforward language. He did not, as you think, very carefully indicate the point you imagine; rather, you are very sleepily examining what he said. You argue that he preferred to say “freed” rather than “free” so that we would understand that freedom of choice enables evil but cannot bring about good. Yet the very order of his words resists you. If he had thought as you do, that freedom produced only sin, he should have said, “You were free for sin”, not “You were free for righteousness” (Romans 6:20), so that a person would be called free with respect to what that freedom accomplished. If we are to weigh even the force of grammatical cases, he said that they were free “for this righteousness”, not free “from this righteousness”. His phrasing would therefore help us more consistently, if we too wished to press such slight matters. Far be it from us! We understand the apostle's meaning and are content with the service of words straightforwardly spoken.

The Teacher of the Nations meant nothing other than: “You were free; you did not serve righteousness. You have been freed; you have received forgiveness of sins.” Freedom of choice remains, through which they could obey sin before and righteousness afterward.

choices.why: Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.
Glossary default: arbitrium is the decision-power, not a later Augustinian/Reformation free-will locus.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

variants.reading: The contrast between “for righteousness” and “from righteousness” reproduces Julian’s argument from Latin grammatical cases. He immediately rejects building his case on that distinction.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
